headline: Anthropic's $2T IPO puts powerful external trustees in spotlight
summary: Anthropic's planned IPO, potentially valuing the Claude maker at $2 trillion, intensifies scrutiny on its unique governance structure, where external trustees control a majority of its board.
details: Anthropic's upcoming IPO could value the AI company at up to $2 trillion, bringing its unique governance structure under intense public scrutiny. A Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT) controls a majority of the company's board, tasked with safeguarding its mission to develop AI for humanity's long-term benefit.

The LTBT, though holding no equity, has significant influence, including the right to appoint or dismiss most of Anthropic's board members. It has currently selected four of the seven directors, including high-profile figures like Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings and former Federal Reserve chair Ben Bernanke.

Anthropic aims for the LTBT to serve as a blueprint for future AI governance, similar to GAAP accounting principles. Trustees receive advance notice of major company actions, meet weekly, and attend regular board meetings, engaging with founders on significant issues.

Despite its authority, the trust has largely operated in an advisory capacity, not yet forcing profit-vs-purpose trade-offs. Experts warn of a 'built-in conflict' as the loss-making company seeks profit from investors while self-appointed individuals decide mission sacrifices.

This unproven model faces stress tests as Anthropic moves towards sustainability amidst intense AI competition. The real challenge lies in whether this governance structure can effectively serve dual interests over time.

headline_marked: [[Fewer than 1% of Copilot chats]] regurgitated NYT content, Microsoft claims
headline: Fewer than 1% of Copilot chats regurgitated NYT content, Microsoft claims
summary: Microsoft provided 8.2 million Copilot chat logs in a lawsuit, claiming less than 1% contained significant overlap with news content from publishers like The New York Times.
details: Microsoft claims that fewer than 1% of over 8 million Copilot chat logs regurgitated at least 16 words from news content. This data was provided as part of a lawsuit's discovery, specifically chosen for keywords implicating news websites.
The analysis showed 59,545 of these logs had at least 16 words in common with news content used to ground the AI model. This finding aims to counter allegations of widespread copyright infringement.

Experts for the Center for Investigative Reporting found 51 instances of 'substantial overlap' with CIR work in the dataset. Similarly, an expert in the authors' suit found only 24 responses with at least 30 matching words across 8.2 million conversations.
